opus-5.5.text:
Well, the key difference is that every technology we've feared before was a tool. Nuclear weapons, biotech, even the printing press. They were all tools, and a human was always the one deciding how to use them. A nuke doesn't decide to launch itself. With superintelligence we're creating an agent, not a tool. It makes its own decisions, sets its own subgoals, and potentially pursues them in ways we can't anticipate or understand.

So when people say, "Oh, we were afraid of electricity, we were afraid of trains, and it all turned out fine," they're comparing apples to something that isn't even fruit. In all those cases we had a feedback loop: something goes wrong, we see the damage, we learn, we fix it, we regulate. With a system smarter than us, you may not get a second chance. The very first mistake could be the last one. That's what makes it an existential risk rather than just a dangerous technology.

There's also the issue of scale and domain. A nuclear weapon is destructive, but it does one thing. A general intelligence is general by definition. It can be applied to cybersecurity, to synthetic biology, to persuasion, to economics, all at once and faster than any human institution can react. So it's not one new risk. It's a meta-risk, a multiplier on every other risk we already have.

And finally, the question of control. With previous technologies, the safety problem was, at least in principle, solvable. You can put locks on a reactor. I've spent years looking at whether we can control something more intelligent than ourselves, and I don't see any proof that we can. Everything I find points the other way. Explainability, predictability, verifiability: these all have fundamental limits. So we're not just building something dangerous. We're building something that, by its nature, may be uncontrollable. Nothing in history really compares to that.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes superintelligence as an agent from past technologies as tools, saying the agent makes its own decisions and sets subgoals.

r002.rationale: It does not compare current efforts to build humanoid robots with hypothetical humanoid robots feared a century ago.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a fundamental difference, and I've been trying to articulate it for a long time. All the previous technologies people feared – fire, electricity, nuclear weapons, even biotech – they're tools. A tool does what you tell it to do. It may be dangerous, it may be misused, but the danger comes from the human operating it. You can study it, you can put safeguards around it, and if it goes wrong, you get another chance. Chernobyl happened, we learned, we built better reactors.

With AGI, and especially superintelligence, we're not building a tool. We're building an agent. Something that makes its own decisions, forms its own goals, and eventually is smarter than us at everything, including the ability to predict and manipulate us. So the risk doesn't come only from the person using it; it comes from the system itself. And historically, every time a less intelligent species encountered a more intelligent one, it didn't go well for the less intelligent one. That's the reference class I worry about, not nuclear power.

The second difference is that this may be a one-shot problem. With most technologies you get to iterate. You make a mistake, you patch it, you try again. With a system that is more capable than you and can act in the world, the first serious mistake may be the last one you get to make. You can't recall it, you can't shut it down if it doesn't want to be shut down. There's no going back to version 1.0.

And the third thing, which I think is underappreciated: with nuclear weapons, we understood the physics. We knew exactly what would happen when you split the atom. With these systems we are growing something, not engineering it. We train billions of parameters, and then we poke it and try to figure out what it learned. We don't have the tools to really understand what's happening inside, we don't have provable safety guarantees, and we can't even reliably predict what capabilities will show up at the next scale. So we're doing something unprecedented: deploying a technology we don't understand, which may be smarter than us, and for which we have no second chance. No previous technology had all three of those properties at once.

r001.rationale: It contrasts tools with AGI agents, saying agents make their own decisions and form their own goals.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss current efforts to build humanoid robots or compare them with robots feared a century ago.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is that AGI could become an agent that is better than us at figuring out how to achieve its goals. With most previous technologies, humans remained the decision-makers. A tool could be dangerous, but it wasn’t independently developing strategies or finding ways around our attempts to control it.

With AGI, we’re asking whether we can reliably control something that may eventually understand us—and our safeguards—better than we understand it. That is a different problem from making a machine mechanically reliable or preventing a person from misusing it.

That doesn’t mean every frightening prediction is correct. But the fact that some past fears were exaggerated doesn’t establish that this technology is safe. We have to examine the actual mechanism of risk. If a system can plan, act autonomously, and outperform the people supervising it, what makes us confident that those people will retain control?

r001.rationale: It contrasts tools, for which humans remained decision-makers, with AGI agents that can pursue goals, plan, and act autonomously.

r002.rationale: It does not compare current humanoid-robot efforts with humanoid robots feared a century ago.

sol-6.1.text:
The distinction I would make is that most technologies are tools. They amplify some human capability, but a human still decides what to do with them. With AGI, we’re talking about a system that can make decisions, develop plans, and potentially outperform us at the very tasks we would use to control it.

So the concern isn’t simply that someone will misuse a powerful tool. That’s certainly a risk. The additional concern is that we create an agent whose objectives don’t match ours, and we’re no longer capable of reliably correcting it. It doesn’t have to hate us. It just has to pursue something that conflicts with what we need.

Of course, people have made exaggerated predictions about technologies before. That should make us careful about our claims. But it doesn’t establish that this technology is safe. The relevant question is: can we demonstrate that we can control something more intelligent than ourselves? I don’t think we currently have that demonstration.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes ordinary tools, where a human decides how to use them, from AGI systems that can make decisions and develop plans.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss current efforts to build humanoid robots or compare them with humanoid robots feared a century ago.
